description: Wildfires affect ecosystems, air quality, and community safety. Our IT team is building an interactive map and calendar that harmonize MODIS and VIIRS satellite hotspot data. Users will be able to explore detections by region, compare recent activity with historical patterns, and identify periods of heightened fire activity.
summary: MODIS and VIIRS fire detections have different resolutions, which complicates comparisons over time. Our project brings these observations together into an interactive map and uses MODIS Aqua as a reference to compare activity across sensors. An experimental model estimates the probability of detecting at least one fire hotspot over the next seven days in grid cells with a history of prior detections.

MODIS and VIIRS instruments detect thermal hotspots at different spatial resolutions. Comparing their counts directly can make differences in detection capability look like changes in fire activity. We built Fire Atlas to bring these observations together in an interactive map and help users explore how activity varies across regions and over time.

Global overview of MODIS and VIIRS detections aggregated into H3 cells, with filters for sensor, region, and time period.

How we compare observations

We use NASA FIRMS data and organize detections into a grid of H3 hexagonal cells. Users can move from a global view to a regional 3D map and select a cell to see detections by sensor, days with available data, and harmonized fire activity. For each individual detection, the API retains the sensor, satellite, data product, and source file.

We also use spatial and temporal proximity to identify potential matches between MODIS and VIIRS detections. Two detections are considered a potential match if they are within 750 meters and 180 minutes of each other. In a test area in Pará, Brazil, 7 of 27 detections were matched using this exploratory criterion.

Detail of an H3 cell in South America, showing the period queried, the days with data, detections per sensor, and harmonized activity.

To compare historical time series, we use MODIS Aqua as a reference and express fire activity in MODIS Aqua–equivalent active cells. This puts observations from both instruments on a common scale. In the calendar, users can select a day to see activity on the map, which satellites contributed observations, and how activity was distributed across brightness temperature ranges. Data availability indicators distinguish days with no available observations from days when observations were available and no activity was detected.

Daily activity in the Marabá region, in Pará, using the satellites they developed, along with the distribution by brightness temperature range.

On the analysis page, the monthly chart shows how harmonized fire activity changes over time. A separate ranking uses detection counts to highlight the cells with the most records in the selected region and period. Historical comparisons require records from at least three prior years. When there is insufficient history, the dashboard marks the comparison as unavailable.

Harmonized activity by month and ranking of cells by number of detections. For the selected view, the dashboard indicates that there is insufficient historical data to calculate a comparison.

How the experimental forecast works

For each covered cell, a tree-based machine learning model estimates the probability of at least one hotspot detection in the seven days after the forecast is issued. It uses recent detections in the cell and its neighbors, along with fire radiative power (FRP) and thermal measurements from the sensors. We used data from 2012 to 2020 for training, data from 2021 and 2022 for parameter tuning, and data from 2023 for testing.

In this version, forecasts are available for cells with a history of detections and sufficient coverage. The dashboard highlights the cells with the highest estimated probabilities and shows when the forecast was issued and where the results came from. These probabilities are experimental, and the model’s evaluation metrics have yet to be published.

Experimental seven-day forecast issued on November 15, 2026, featuring the cells with the highest estimated probability, along with the forecast's metadata.

How data reaches the application

Amazon S3, an AWS service, is the foundation of the Fire Atlas data infrastructure. It hosts the data lake where we publish the detections and processed datasets that power the application. The Silver layer stores individual detections. The Gold layer contains the map grid, place names, harmonized time series, and experimental forecasts.

We use Delta Lake and Parquet to organize the datasets, DuckDB to read the files, and PostgreSQL with PostGIS to store and query geospatial records. Our Spring Boot REST API queries the database to serve the map, calendar, analysis page, and forecast dashboard. When the API starts, it synchronizes the Gold layer with Amazon S3 in the background.

Fire Atlas helps users monitoring a region trace records to their source, check whether observations were available, and track changes in fire activity on a common scale. The experimental forecast lets them explore where new hotspots may be detected over the following seven days.
